paragraphs: Learning a fast surrogate for a partial differential equation requires training examples from an expensive numerical solver. Active learning tries to spend that simulation budget on useful examples. This paper changes the unit of acquisition: instead of always paying for a complete trajectory through time, it selects particular time steps within trajectories.

The numerical solver generates the selected steps, while the surrogate approximates the others. Reducing the cost of each trajectory lets the learning process explore a more diverse collection under the same budget. To choose steps, the authors develop an acquisition function that estimates how much a set of observations would reduce predictive variance.

Experiments cover Burgers’, Korteweg–De Vries, Kuramoto–Sivashinsky, and both incompressible and compressible Navier–Stokes equations. The authors report large improvements over the strongest existing method, including lower average error and lower error at the 50th, 95th, and 99th percentiles. These results indicate improvements across the error distribution, extending beyond better average predictions to the more difficult cases represented by its upper tail.
icml-2025-active-learning-with-selective.tldr: Selecting individual simulation time steps makes active learning for PDE surrogates more data-efficient and improves errors across tested benchmarks.

paragraphs: Class-incremental learning asks a model to learn new classes while retaining earlier ones. Replaying stored examples can reduce forgetting and confusion between tasks, but storing and processing those examples becomes increasingly costly as tasks accumulate. This paper proposes autoencoder-based hybrid replay to reduce the storage burden.

Its hybrid autoencoder compresses examples into a latent representation, which is stored instead of raw data. A decoder later reconstructs examples for replay. The same architecture supports classification and generation, connecting the representation used to distinguish classes with the representation used to recover old examples. To accommodate new classes, it arranges class centers using energy minimization and repulsion inspired by charged particles.

The reported worst-case storage expression is O(0.1t), while computation remains O(t). The storage claim therefore concerns a smaller constant factor, with growth still linear in task count. Across multiple benchmarks, the method consistently outperforms recent baselines under equal memory and computation budgets. The findings support compressed replay as a way to retain useful past experience more economically.
icml-2025-autoencoder-based-hybrid-repla.tldr: A hybrid autoencoder stores compressed replay examples and organizes class representations to improve incremental learning within limited resources.

paragraphs: Post-training quantization makes large language models easier to deploy by representing their numerical values with reduced precision. Choosing those values carefully matters for accuracy. The paper addresses a tradeoff in existing approaches: gradient-based optimization can be expensive at large scale, while cheaper alternatives may overlook interactions between layers or rely on simple nearest-value rounding.

BoA optimizes quantized weights without backpropagation while accounting for dependencies inside attention modules. Its central tool is an attention-aware Hessian matrix, which represents how interacting changes affect the optimization objective. Including this interaction information lets the algorithm make weight assignments with more context than an isolated rounding decision provides.

The experiments report better performance than existing weight quantization methods. BoA also works well with conventional techniques for suppressing unusually large activations, producing state-of-the-art results for quantizing both weights and activations. The contribution is therefore both an optimization method and evidence that attention-specific dependency information can improve quantization without requiring the gradient-based procedure that motivates the computational concern.
icml-2025-boa-attention-aware-post-train.tldr: BoA improves post-training quantization by modeling attention-layer interactions while optimizing weights without backpropagation.

paragraphs: Different language models may appear to offer independent perspectives because they have different architectures, training histories, or providers. This paper asks whether those differences translate into meaningfully different errors. The authors evaluate more than 350 models overall using two popular leaderboards and a resume-screening task.

They find substantial correlation between mistakes. On one leaderboard dataset, pairs of models agree 60% of the time when both are wrong. That figure is conditional on both models making an error; it does not describe their overall error rate. Shared architectures and providers help explain correlation, but larger and more accurate models also show highly correlated errors across those boundaries.

The study then examines consequences for evaluation with language-model judges and for hiring decisions. The hiring findings reflect theoretical predictions about algorithmic monoculture, where similar automated decisions create shared patterns of outcomes. The central implication is that model variety and individual accuracy do not by themselves establish diversity of behavior: understanding shared mistakes requires measuring those mistakes directly.
icml-2025-correlated-errors-in-large-lan.tldr: An evaluation of over 350 LLMs finds substantial shared errors, including among accurate models from different providers and architectures.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization guides the search for good inputs when evaluating a function is expensive. A common approach predicts function values probabilistically. This paper builds on an alternative that separates observations into relatively promising and less promising groups, then uses density ratios or classification probabilities to guide the search.

The authors identify overconfidence in supervised classifiers as a problem for this approach. A classifier can be too certain about what the available evaluations reveal about global solution candidates. Their proposed method introduces semi-supervised learning, allowing the model to use candidate inputs whose function values have not been evaluated as well as the labeled observations.

Access to these unlabeled points is an explicit assumption, with a predefined pool offered as one example. The experiments examine both sampled unlabeled points and a fixed-size pool, comparing the proposed methods with several baselines. The stated contribution is a way to incorporate unevaluated inputs into classifier-based optimization and an empirical investigation of its validity across varied experiments; the abstract does not claim a quantified or universal improvement.
icml-2025-density-ratio-estimation-based.tldr: Semi-supervised learning incorporates unevaluated candidate inputs into density-ratio-based Bayesian optimization to address classifier overconfidence.

paragraphs: Zero-shot text-to-speech systems can reproduce a voice from very little audio. This paper studies how to selectively remove a trained system’s ability to imitate designated speakers while preserving useful synthesis for others. The target is speaker identity knowledge within the model, making the task a form of machine unlearning.

The authors introduce unlearning frameworks for this setting, particularly Teacher-Guided Unlearning. Their methods incorporate randomness to prevent consistent reproduction of the speakers selected for forgetting. The intended change is selective: prompts associated with those speakers should no longer recover their identities, while speech generation for retained speakers should remain accurate.

The paper also proposes speaker-Zero Retrain Forgetting, an evaluation metric for whether the model disregards prompts tied to forgotten identities. Experiments on a state-of-the-art speech model show that Teacher-Guided Unlearning prevents replication of the designated voices while maintaining high quality for others. These findings establish an experimental approach to voice-specific removal and a corresponding way to evaluate whether identity prompts still influence synthesis.
icml-2025-do-not-mimic-my-voice-speaker-.tldr: Teacher-Guided Unlearning selectively suppresses designated voice identities in zero-shot speech synthesis while preserving quality for other speakers.

paragraphs: A vision transformer trained on natural images may need additional adaptation when its target images come from a different domain. ExPLoRA investigates whether this adjustment can begin through efficient self-supervised pretraining on unlabeled target-domain data. This extends parameter-efficient adaptation to the stage before supervised task training.

Starting with pretrained weights such as DinoV2 or MAE, the method continues unsupervised training on the new domain. It fully updates one or two transformer blocks and uses low-rank adaptation, or LoRA, for the remaining layers. The resulting model then undergoes supervised fine-tuning using only LoRA. This sequence combines a limited amount of full-block flexibility with broadly distributed low-rank updates.

Experiments on satellite imagery report state-of-the-art performance, including results exceeding full pretraining and fine-tuning. With the DinoV2 objective, the authors report up to 8% improvement in linear-probing top-1 accuracy while updating fewer than 10% as many parameters as prior fully tuned approaches. Ablations support the proposed design, suggesting that economical domain adaptation can benefit from extending pretraining itself.
icml-2025-explora-parameter-efficient-ex.tldr: ExPLoRA adapts vision transformers to new domains through mostly low-rank self-supervised pretraining followed by LoRA fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines updates from clients whose data may have very different distributions. Local training can become too specialized to a client, and combining updates can distort features that would otherwise transfer well. FedCONST addresses both problems by controlling how strongly different parts of the model are updated.

The method adapts update magnitudes according to the global model’s parameter strength. It reduces emphasis on parameters that are already well learned and reinforces those that remain underdeveloped. Linear convex constraints provide the mechanism for stabilizing training and preserving the generalization capabilities acquired locally when client contributions are aggregated.

The authors use Gradient Signal-to-Noise Ratio analysis to support the method’s effect on feature transferability and robustness. They also report state-of-the-art performance across diverse federated learning environments. Together, these findings connect the update rule to the central coordination problem: local learning should contribute useful features to the shared model without allowing differences between client distributions to drive excessive specialization or erase transferable information during aggregation.
icml-2025-federated-learning-for-feature.tldr: FedCONST constrains and scales client updates to preserve transferable features and improve generalization in federated learning.

paragraphs: Animating clipart requires both coherent shapes and smooth changes over time. A method can produce plausible individual deformations yet still create abrupt movement or geometric distortion between frames. The paper also identifies a mismatch between clipart and the natural-video statistics learned by text-to-video and image-to-video models.

FlexiClip extends motion trajectories built from Bézier curves with three mechanisms. Temporal Jacobians incrementally correct motion dynamics. Probability flow ordinary differential equations model motion continuously to reduce temporal noise. A flow-matching loss inspired by GFlowNet principles further encourages smooth transitions. These components connect the handling of spatial deformation with the handling of motion through time.

The method integrates this modeling with pretrained video diffusion models. Experiments report smooth, natural, and structurally consistent animations across varied clipart, including human and animal characters, with complex cases involving rapid motion and non-rigid deformation. The findings support treating temporal coherence and geometric integrity as coupled requirements, so improvements in motion do not come at the expense of the character’s visual structure.
icml-2025-flexiclip-locality-preserving-.tldr: FlexiClip combines geometric deformation and continuous-time motion modeling to produce smoother, structurally consistent clipart animations.

paragraphs: Quantizing a language model reduces the precision of its weights or activations to lower memory requirements and inference latency. The paper argues that good quantization decisions need two kinds of information: how much hidden features matter to the final loss, and how changes to different weights interact with one another.

GuidedQuant brings gradients from the final loss into its quantization objective while retaining dependencies between weights within output channels. This connects local numerical approximations to their importance for the model’s end objective. Preserving weight interactions also avoids treating every weight change as if its effect could be assessed independently.

The authors report consistent improvements to state-of-the-art methods across weight-only scalar quantization, weight-only vector quantization, and joint weight-and-activation quantization. They additionally introduce a non-uniform scalar quantization algorithm that is guaranteed to monotonically decrease its quantization objective and outperforms existing methods in that category. That guarantee concerns the specified optimization objective; the broader performance improvements are supported by the reported experiments across quantization settings.
icml-2025-guidedquant-large-language-mod.tldr: GuidedQuant improves LLM quantization by combining final-loss gradients with dependencies between weights.

paragraphs: Long-horizon reinforcement learning becomes difficult when rewards provide little guidance until late in a task. Hierarchical methods address this by organizing behavior around intermediate subgoals. This paper focuses on discovering the relationships between those subgoals and using that structure to make exploration more efficient.

The authors represent the subgoal hierarchy as a causal graph and introduce an algorithm to discover it. The learned graph then guides which subgoals to intervene on during exploration. Interventions are prioritized according to their importance for reaching the final goal, so exploration uses the discovered structure rather than choosing subgoal interventions randomly.

The paper provides formal analysis showing improvements for tree structures and a variant of Erdős–Rényi random graphs. These graph families define the scope of the stated theoretical results. Experiments on hierarchical reinforcement-learning tasks also show lower training cost than existing work. The combined contribution links learning a causal structure with acting on it: the hierarchy becomes a practical guide for allocating training effort toward subgoals relevant to success.
icml-2025-hierarchical-reinforcement-lea.tldr: Learning causal relationships between subgoals helps hierarchical reinforcement learning target useful interventions and reduce training cost.

paragraphs: Results favoring permutation-based stochastic gradient methods have largely concerned training for more epochs than the problem’s condition number. This paper investigates the less understood regime where the epoch count is smaller. It studies Incremental Gradient Descent, a deterministic member of this family, on smooth, strongly convex objectives.

The authors establish lower bounds showing that convergence can be surprisingly slow in this regime, even when every component function is strongly convex. Allowing some components to be nonconvex can make the optimality gap substantially worse throughout the small-epoch regime. Thus, favorable properties of the overall objective do not eliminate the importance of assumptions about its individual components.

These are worst-case statements about how slowly IGD can converge, rather than claims that every training run behaves poorly. The paper also supplies matching upper and lower bounds for the large-epoch regime. Together, the results clarify why advantages established after many passes through the data cannot simply be carried over to short runs, and why component-level assumptions matter when analyzing permutation-based methods.
icml-2025-incremental-gradient-descent-w.tldr: Lower bounds show that deterministic incremental gradient descent can converge very slowly when epoch counts are below the condition number.

paragraphs: An inhomogeneous Poisson process describes events whose occurrence intensity varies across the domain. Estimating that intensity can use either classical kernel intensity estimators or kernel methods formulated in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. Despite sharing the word kernel, these approaches originate from different theoretical principles.

The paper connects them through a regularized least-squares formulation for Poisson processes. Its solution satisfies a specialized representer theorem with a dual coefficient equal to one and coincides with a classical kernel intensity estimator. This establishes a precise mathematical relationship between the two families rather than relying on their similar terminology.

The connection enables the authors to apply techniques from reproducing kernel Hilbert space theory to construct K²IE, an efficient intensity estimator. On synthetic datasets, it achieves predictive performance comparable to a state-of-the-art kernel-method estimator while substantially improving computational efficiency. The result matters in two ways: it explains how a familiar estimator emerges from an optimization framework, and it uses that explanation to obtain a more efficient implementation with competitive predictions.
icml-2025-k-2-ie-kernel-method-based-ker.tldr: K²IE connects classical intensity estimation with RKHS optimization and uses that connection to improve computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Low-rank adaptation is widely used to fine-tune foundation models, but explaining its optimization behavior remains difficult. Earlier theoretical accounts often depend on linear approximations or highly simplified settings. This paper analyzes the LoRA loss landscape while distinguishing situations where those approximations hold from more realistic ones where they do not.

The authors call these the special and generic regimes. In the generic regime, their result identifies two qualitatively different outcomes: convergence to a global minimizer with low rank and small magnitude, or convergence to a solution with high rank and large magnitude. The distinction makes the alternative to the favorable outcome structurally recognizable in the analysis.

The paper then argues that zero-initialization and weight decay bias training toward the low-rank, small-magnitude region containing global minima. This provides an explanation for why LoRA often succeeds, while preserving the theorem’s alternative outcome. The practical interpretation is that training choices may favor the desirable part of the landscape; the abstract does not establish that every LoRA run necessarily reaches a global minimum.
icml-2025-lora-training-provably-converg.tldr: The analysis separates favorable LoRA convergence from a structurally distinct alternative and argues that common training choices favor global minima.

paragraphs: Audio-visual speech recognition combines sound and visual information to improve recognition in noisy environments. Increasing model capacity can help, but existing systems face a computational challenge when scaling up. MoHAVE addresses that challenge with a mixture-of-experts architecture designed around the two input modalities.

The framework organizes experts into modality-specific groups and uses hierarchical gating to select them according to the input context. Because the mixture is sparse, the model can expand its available capacity while activating only selected experts. The gating mechanism connects computational allocation to the audio-visual evidence available for a particular input, supporting adaptation with limited additional overhead.

The authors report strong performance on robust audio-visual benchmarks, including LRS3 and MuAViC transcription and translation tasks. The contribution combines the architecture for scaling capacity with a routing mechanism intended to preserve efficiency and robustness. Its stated findings support context-dependent use of specialized expert groups as a way to handle varied audio-visual inputs while avoiding the computational burden of using all model capacity on every example.
icml-2025-mohave-mixture-of-hierarchical.tldr: MoHAVE routes audio-visual inputs through selected expert groups to scale robust speech recognition with limited computational overhead.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning seeks to remove selected knowledge from an already trained model. One approach fine-tunes on the data to be forgotten, measures the resulting weight change, and subtracts that change from the original model. Its effectiveness can depend strongly on which fine-tuning hyperparameters produced the chosen change vector.

NegMerge uses the collection of models trained with different hyperparameters instead of selecting a single candidate. It forms their task vectors and retains elements whose signs agree across them. The merged vector is then negated and applied to the original model. Agreement in update direction becomes the criterion for deciding which parts of the candidate changes to use.

Evaluations span zero-shot and standard image recognition across twelve datasets and four backbone architectures. The authors report improvements over state-of-the-art unlearning methods with similar or lower computational requirements. The results support extracting a shared direction from multiple fine-tuning runs as an alternative to extensive validation for one optimal candidate, while using the same basic idea of reversing a learned weight change.
icml-2025-negmerge-sign-consensual-weigh.tldr: NegMerge combines sign-consistent weight changes from multiple fine-tuned models and reverses the merged direction to induce unlearning.

paragraphs: A trained generative model can be paired with search at test time to improve the candidates it produces. Neural Genetic Search applies this idea to discrete spaces by incorporating the evolutionary mechanism of genetic algorithms into generation. The paper’s focus is the search procedure used with trained models.

Its central innovation is the crossover operation. NGS defines crossover as generation conditioned on parent candidates, with the trained generative model producing the resulting candidate. This makes the model part of the mechanism for combining information from parents. The proposal connects evolutionary search to model-based generation through an operation that can be applied across different kinds of discrete outputs.

The authors demonstrate the method on routing problems, adversarial prompt generation for language models, and molecular design. These domains provide evidence for the method’s flexibility as well as its effectiveness. The abstract characterizes NGS as versatile and easy to implement. Its main contribution is a reusable way to organize test-time search around parent-conditioned generation, supported by experiments across three distinct application areas.
icml-2025-neural-genetic-search-in-discr.tldr: Neural Genetic Search uses parent-conditioned generation as crossover to improve test-time search in discrete spaces.

paragraphs: Auction guarantees often rely on assumptions about how bidder values are distributed. This paper asks how learning algorithms can provide useful assurances when those assumptions themselves may be questionable. It adapts testable learning, where the outcome is either a performance guarantee or evidence that the assumed distributional conditions fail.

The authors show that regularity, a common assumption in mechanism design, cannot be tested within the original framework. They introduce a regularized framework with a different benchmark: either the learner earns high revenue relative to the best achievable revenue of a nearby regular distribution, or it determines that the input distribution is not regular.

Within this framework, the paper provides a tester paired with a learner for revenue-optimal mechanisms. It also develops a test for whether the Bulow–Klemperer theorem applies to a dataset and a test confirming the existence of an anonymous reserve price securing a constant fraction of optimal revenue. The nearby-distribution comparison is central: it defines the revenue assurance that makes this revised form of testable mechanism design possible.
icml-2025-safely-learning-optimal-auctio.tldr: A regularized testable-learning framework offers auction revenue guarantees against nearby regular distributions or detects failure of regularity.

paragraphs: Gradient-based bilevel optimization involves an optimization problem whose outcome feeds into another optimization problem. Applications include tuning hyperparameters, adapting to tasks, and discovering learning algorithms. Computing the outer update can require differentiating through the inner training procedure, creating expensive derivatives of calculations that already contain gradients.

Automatic differentiation makes those calculations convenient to express, but the paper argues that standard implementations often miss opportunities created by the structure of these problems. The authors analyze such cases and introduce Mixed-Flow Meta-Gradients, or MixFlow-MG. It combines differentiation modes to construct more efficient computational graphs for obtaining the required meta-gradients.

In modern meta-learning setups, the authors report memory improvements exceeding a factor of ten and wall-clock time improvements of up to 25% over standard implementations. These are distinct resource benefits: reducing the graph’s memory demands addresses scalability, while reducing elapsed time makes the computation faster. The contribution shows that how a nested derivative calculation is organized can materially affect its practical cost, even when automatic differentiation already provides a working implementation.
icml-2025-scalable-meta-learning-via-mix.tldr: MixFlow-MG reorganizes meta-gradient computation with mixed-mode differentiation, reporting over tenfold memory improvements and up to 25% faster execution.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a language model infer a task from its prompt. This paper uses sparse autoencoders to investigate the internal features involved in that process. The goal is to show that these tools can address a mechanistic question about model behavior, beyond offering descriptions of individual activations.

The authors identify features that encode which task to execute. Interventions using their latent vectors can causally induce the task without examples, connecting these features to earlier accounts based on task vectors. They also show that task vectors can be approximated well by sparse combinations of autoencoder latents, including the identified task-execution features.

To trace how these signals arise, the authors scale sparse feature circuit analysis to Gemma 1 2B. They discover earlier-activating features that detect when tasks have been performed in the prompt. Attention and MLP sublayers causally connect those detecting features to task-execution features. The findings provide a more detailed account linking recognition of demonstrated tasks to the internal signals that guide subsequent task performance.
icml-2025-scaling-sparse-feature-circuit.tldr: Sparse feature circuits reveal causally connected task-detection and task-execution features involved in in-context learning.

paragraphs: Reducing the number of trainable parameters can lower fine-tuning memory requirements without reducing the computation needed to train a language model. The paper notes that parameter-efficient methods can even slow training in some cases. SparseLoRA targets computation directly by selecting which weights participate in loss and gradient calculations.

The selection uses a lightweight estimator based on singular value decomposition that requires no training of its own. It dynamically identifies a sparse subset of weights according to context. The authors also analyze and address differences in sensitivity across layers, tokens, and training steps, making the selection responsive to where and when sparsity is applied.

Experiments report computational cost reductions of up to 2.2 times and measured speedups of up to 1.6 times while maintaining accuracy. The evaluated tasks include commonsense reasoning, arithmetic reasoning, code generation, and instruction following. The separate figures distinguish reduced computation from realized elapsed-time gains. The results support contextual sparsity as a way to add practical acceleration to parameter-efficient fine-tuning, beyond reducing how many parameters are updated.
icml-2025-sparselora-accelerating-llm-fi.tldr: SparseLoRA dynamically limits fine-tuning computation to selected weights, achieving measured speedups of up to 1.6 times while maintaining accuracy.

paragraphs: Distributing a large language model across multiple computing units introduces communication costs as well as computational capacity. In tensor parallelism, synchronization between units can become a bottleneck for inference latency. Sync-Point Drop addresses this by selectively removing synchronization associated with attention outputs.

The authors first design a block that can continue execution without the communication removed by SPD. They then assign different dropping strategies to attention blocks according to how sensitive those blocks are to model accuracy. This makes synchronization removal selective, connecting the communication savings to the model’s tolerance for changes at particular locations.

For LLaMA2-70B inference across eight GPUs, SPD reduces overall inference latency by about 20% with less than 1% accuracy regression. This result demonstrates a measured communication-versus-accuracy tradeoff in the stated configuration. The broader contribution is a way to treat synchronization points as optimization targets, using block design and sensitivity analysis together to reduce distributed inference overhead while limiting the resulting degradation in model performance.
icml-2025-spd-sync-point-drop-for-effici.tldr: SPD selectively drops attention-output synchronization, reducing LLaMA2-70B inference latency by about 20% across eight GPUs with under 1% accuracy regression.

paragraphs: Cell microscopy representations need to capture biological effects despite random and systematic measurement errors. This paper presents a three-part pretraining strategy: curate diverse, internally consistent samples, scale an appropriate foundation model on them, and inspect intermediate layers to identify the representations most useful for downstream tasks.

Using this strategy, the authors train a 1.9-billion-parameter ViT-G/8 masked autoencoder on more than eight billion microscopy image crops. They describe it as the largest cell-microscopy foundation model to their knowledge. The framework treats data consistency and representation selection as explicit parts of scaling, alongside the model’s size and training dataset.

Compared with a previously published ViT-L/8 masked autoencoder, the model improves linear separability of genetic perturbations by 60%, meaning the learned representations better support separating those perturbations with a linear decision rule. It also achieves the best overall performance on the reported whole-genome relationship recall, batch-correction replicate consistency, and compound–gene activity prediction benchmarks. These results connect the pretraining strategy to several distinct tests of biological usefulness.
icml-2025-vitally-consistent-scaling-bio.tldr: A microscopy pretraining framework combining consistent data, model scaling, and layer selection improves biological representations across several benchmarks.

paragraphs: CLIP’s ability to generalize is often credited to diverse training data, but diversity alone leaves important questions unresolved. This paper distinguishes transfer to an entirely unseen domain from recognizing unseen classes within a domain that was only partly represented during training. These correspond to domain and compositional generalization.

The authors train CLIP models on deliberately constructed data distributions that control domain diversity and exposure to object classes. In these experiments, domain diversity is essential for both forms of generalization. Yet partial familiarity with a test domain can be associated with surprisingly weaker compositional generalization than transfer to an entirely unseen domain when the observed subset is suboptimal.

Data-focused and mechanistic analyses connect successful generalization to sufficiently shared representations in intermediate layers and circuits. This provides an internal explanation alongside the training-data findings. The study indicates that assessing generalization requires attention to which combinations of domains and classes the model sees, as well as whether its internal representations capture information shared across them.
icml-2025-when-and-how-does-clip-enable-.tldr: Controlled CLIP experiments link generalization to domain diversity and shared internal representations, while showing that partial domain exposure can be problematic.

paragraphs: Data-free image synthesis aims to recover images resembling a pretrained model’s learned distribution without accessing its original training data. The paper identifies limited knowledge of natural images as a reason existing methods produce mismatched samples. DDIS addresses this by using a text-to-image diffusion model as an image prior.

The method extracts distributional knowledge from the given pretrained model and uses it to guide image generation. Domain Alignment Guidance steers diffusion sampling toward the original training domain. Separately, an optimized Class Alignment Token embedding captures class-specific attributes. These components address both the broader characteristics of the source domain and the details associated with individual classes.

Experiments on PACS and ImageNet show that DDIS generates samples that better reflect the training distribution than earlier data-free synthesis methods. The authors also report state-of-the-art performance in data-free applications. The findings support combining a diffusion model’s image-generation prior with knowledge retained in another trained model, using explicit domain and class alignment to make synthetic data relevant to that model’s unavailable training set.
icml-2025-when-model-knowledge-meets-dif.tldr: DDIS guides a diffusion model with domain and class knowledge from a pretrained model to synthesize better-aligned images without original training data.
